For repair, edit-operation F1 is reported separately. NN-Residual F1 . As we’ve seen in Section 3.3 , a simple nearest-neighbor policy skews the link evaluation into easy instances. Hence, a weak tracker naturally learns to link the behaviors of the nearest neighbors but fails at harder instances, which might require more cognitive effort. Nearest-neighbor (NN) matching is therefore a necessary solving policy for a tracker, but not sufficient. The NN-Residual F1 metric is an attempt to remove the NN bias from the evaluation by sampling the F1 score only on links that are not explained by such heuristic. The primary, shortcut-resistance, and graph-level results are summarized in Table 2 . The nearest-centroid baseline achieves LNK sub of 0.493, showing that cell linking can already be solved relatively well by proximity alone. The only models to overcome this baseline are GPT-5.6 (sol), with 0.767 0.767 ( Δ \Delta NN + 0.274 +0.274 ), followed by GPT-5.6 (terra), Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.5, and Claude Opus 5; and Claude Opus 4.8, which is nearly equal to the NN baseline (+0.009). All open-weight models stay below it. The aggregate linking F1 can shadow real deficiencies, justifying the proposed metrics. For example, Gemma 4 31B is the most powerful open-weight model with a Link F1 of 0.641, almost matching the specialized trackers, but its LNK sub is 0.484, and its NN-residual and division F1 scores are only 0.149 and 0.103, respectively.

This suggests that this model and other open-weight models perform well because they rely on proximity for matching. In contrast, the best-performing model on these metrics, GPT-5.6 (sol), scores an NN-residual F1 of 0.723 and a division F1 of 0.787. It is important to note that low tracker scores do not indicate anything about their full-sequence performance, since the benchmark problems were deliberately chosen to be ones where these trackers fail. Can VLMs repair tracker output? Appendix Table 8 decomposes repair behavior by edit type and per-neighborhood graph. Repair F1 measures how much of the proposed graph is correct after editing, but not whether the model improves the graph. For that, we rely on Δ \Delta LNK. GPT-5.6 (sol) is the most useful, raising LNK by +0.412 and improving 80% of the cases while worsening only 7% and 13% kept unchanged. On the other hand, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B achieves a repair F1 of 0.622, but its LNK is increased only by +0.008, mostly because it doesn’t change the proposed graph. Even more, Molmo2-8B and Llama 4 Scout have repair F1 scores of 0.521 and 0.342, respectively, while changing LNK by -0.099 and -0.385. Six of the 13 open-weight models actually hurt performance and give a negative Δ \Delta LNK. For that reason, repair must be interpreted by graph improvement, edit precision, and recall. Can VLMs prioritize human review? Appendix Table 9 evaluates inspection under fixed review budgets. Inspection is only useful if it identifies errors early enough to reduce human effort. We therefore cap flags at a fixed review budget and simulate the correction of the selected sources. Under the most restrictive budget, the frontier models achieve a recovery of Δ \Delta LNK between +0.235 and +0.249, which is 83–88% of the gold oracle’s +0.284 and almost twice that of a random reviewer (+0.125). However, the model can produce indiscriminate flags.

For example, Llama 4 Scout produces 3,061 flags and recovers +0.519, but it achieves only +0.117 when the tighter budget is applied, which is below random selection. Therefore, inspection must be analyzed according to the review budget, and not only by the improvement when examining all the flags. Difficulty factors and task relationships. Proximity resistance is the hardest challenge. The nearest-centroid rule solves just 22 out of 244 problems exactly. All models do well on these 22, but their performance drops on the other 222. For these NN-resistant cases, LNK sub is 0.766 0.766 for GPT-5.6 (sol) and 0.536 0.536 for Gemma 4 31B. Weaker models also struggle more with divisions. The mining-hardness score shows another side of difficulty (Appendix Table 10 ). Performance usually drops as we move to harder groups, but not for every model. The hard-mining procedure shapes how the benchmark is chosen: all three trackers agree on 235 out of 244 test neighborhoods. This means the benchmark focuses on consistently tough cases. Because of this, there is little variation, so proximity resistance and division metrics help sort the cases more clearly. The three tasks are related but have different roles. Linking and repair scores are closely tied across models (Spearman ρ = 0.85 \rho=0.85 ), so models that rebuild associations well also fix them well. Inspection is less connected, with a Spearman of ρ = 0.51 \rho=0.51 with linking and ρ = 0.29 \rho=0.29 with repair. This shows that finding links to review is a separate skill. Each task, therefore, highlights a unique way a VLM can support the tracking process. Interface and inference efficiency. The harness selection study benefited from coordinate-based interfaces with model-requested crops in a multi-turn fashion over fixed supplied crops in a single-turn fashion. For GPT-5.5, c1 performs the best; meanwhile, Claude Opus 4.8 favors the more information-rich c8 configuration.

This model-dependent order suggests that both harnesses provide access to the visual evidence effectively; meanwhile, different models use the additional segmentation delineation cues differently. We selected c1 and froze it for the final testing, ensuring that every model is evaluated equally. A validation-test comparison under the frozen protocol is reported in Appendix Table 7 . Moreover, through a fixed inference budget, we measured how effectively a model can complete the task within a reasonable amount of time. This provides interesting insights into some open-weight models. For example, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B responses are truncated in 87% of problems, even with the final low-context warning. In contrast, larger variants are truncated by ≈ \approx 40%. This reflects inference efficiency, a key concern in a tool-using setting. 5 Conclusion We introduced CellTrack-Bench, a benchmark for assessing vision-language models (VLMs) for cell tracking by breaking long tracking sequences into compact, digestible tasks for current models. Given the skewed distribution of mistakes, we selected difficult associations from common mistakes made by specialized trackers and formulated three complementary tasks: cell linking, track repair, and track inspection. Our formulation lets us evaluate whether VLMs can directly restore cell associations, fix existing tracking solutions, or prioritize likely mistakes for review during human data curation. Our results suggest that advanced VLMs possess abilities that go beyond mere geometric tricks. The most advanced VLMs, the closed-source frontier models, can operate without nearest-neighbor shortcuts, improve poorly performing tracker solutions, and prioritize tracker errors even under limited inspection budgets. However, these abilities are not universal: weaker models still rely on the proximity shortcut and, in some cases, can even worsen tracking performance during repair.

Taken together, these facts suggest that, for now, VLMs are better used as reasoning modules in the cell-tracking pipeline rather than as substitutes for specialized trackers. We expect our CellTrack-Bench to serve as an evaluation setting for developing VLMs capable of cognitive reasoning about complex biological events, where specialized trackers often make mistakes.
